summary: Psalm 3 begins with a speaker surrounded by many adversaries and by voices saying that God will not help him. The poem moves from complaint to trust, from a cry for rescue to a final claim that salvation belongs to Yahweh and blessing is sought for the people.
whyItMatters: This chapter stands near the beginning of Book I, where David-associated prayers of danger and confidence are prominent. It shows the Psalter teaching prayer that can name threat plainly while still turning toward God for help.

context.author: Many writers and collections stand behind Psalms. The heading of this psalm associates it with David when he fled from Absalom his son, but the book briefing notes that Davidic headings are debated and may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Psalms is a curated anthology of Hebrew poetry and prayer. This chapter speaks from danger, opposition, and trust, with attention to Yahweh's holy hill.
context.literaryForm: Highly compressed Hebrew poetry and prayer, with parallel lines, direct address to Yahweh, and the repeated performance marker Selah.

outline.heading: The heading and the crisis
outline.note: The psalm is associated with David's flight from Absalom, and the speaker says adversaries have multiplied.

outline.heading: Many deny help
outline.note: The speaker reports that many say there is no help for him in God, followed by Selah.

outline.heading: Yahweh as shield and answerer
outline.note: The speaker addresses Yahweh as protection, glory, and the one who answers from his holy hill.

outline.heading: Sleep without fear
outline.note: The speaker says he slept and awakened because Yahweh sustains him, and he will not fear thousands surrounding him.

outline.heading: A plea for rescue
outline.note: The speaker calls on Yahweh to arise and save, using violent images of enemies struck and the wicked disabled.

outline.heading: Salvation and blessing
outline.note: The psalm ends by locating salvation with Yahweh and asking blessing for Yahweh's people.

keyVerses.text: Many there are who say of my soul, “There is no help for him in God.” Selah.
keyVerses.why: This states the pressure around the speaker: opposition includes a claim that God will not help him.

keyVerses.text: But you, Yahweh, are a shield around me, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.
keyVerses.why: This is the main turn from what the many say to what the speaker says about Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for Yahweh sustains me.
keyVerses.why: The danger has not disappeared, but the speaker describes being preserved through the night.

keyVerses.text: Salvation belongs to Yahweh. May your blessing be on your people. Selah.
keyVerses.why: The final line widens the prayer from the speaker's rescue to Yahweh's people.

questions.question: What does the first line before the prayer do?
questions.answer: Verse 1 is a heading that associates the psalm with David when he fled from Absalom his son. The book briefing says such headings are ancient features of the Psalter, but their exact force is debated; readers differ on whether this one should be treated as authorship, historical association, or later framing. The guide should therefore notice the heading without turning it into more certainty than the briefing provides.

questions.question: Who are the “adversaries” in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter itself does not name them beyond the heading's reference to Absalom. In the body of the psalm, they are described as many people who rise up, speak against the speaker's soul, and set themselves against him on every side. The text emphasizes the scale and pressure of opposition more than their individual identities.

questions.question: What is “Selah”?
questions.answer: Selah appears in verses 2, 4, and 8. The book briefing identifies it as an uncertain musical or performance marker, often preserved in translation because its exact instruction is no longer known. In this chapter it marks pauses at major points: after the hostile claim, after Yahweh's answer, and after the final blessing.

questions.question: Does verse 2 mean the speaker has lost faith?
questions.answer: Verse 2 reports what “many” say about the speaker: “There is no help for him in God.” The next verses answer that claim by addressing Yahweh as shield, glory, and the one who lifts up the speaker's head. The chapter presents the hostile claim and the speaker's trust side by side.

questions.question: What does “holy hill” refer to here?
questions.answer: Verse 4 says Yahweh answers the speaker “out of his holy hill.” The chapter does not explain the phrase, but the book briefing says many psalms are oriented toward Jerusalem and its temple. It is safest to say the phrase evokes Yahweh's sacred place without reconstructing a precise ritual scene from this verse alone.

questions.question: Why is sleeping important in the middle of danger?
questions.answer: Verse 5 says, “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened, for Yahweh sustains me.” Verse 6 then says the speaker will not be afraid of tens of thousands surrounding him. The sleep is not proof that the danger is gone; it is the speaker's testimony that Yahweh has preserved him within it.

questions.question: Is verse 7 asking for revenge?
questions.answer: Verse 7 asks Yahweh to arise and save, and it uses harsh images: enemies struck on the cheek bone and the teeth of the wicked broken. Readers differ on how to use such lines: some stress that the speaker hands judgment to Yahweh rather than acting directly, while others emphasize the moral difficulty of praying violent imagery. The chapter itself presents the plea as part of a prayer from danger, not as a general permission for personal retaliation.

questions.question: Why does the ending mention “your people” instead of only the speaker?
questions.answer: Most of the psalm speaks in the first person: “my adversaries,” “my voice,” and “I will not be afraid.” Verse 8 broadens the horizon: “May your blessing be on your people.” The speaker's need for rescue is placed within a wider concern for the people who belong to Yahweh.

glossary.def: Opponents or enemies; in verse 1 they have increased and rise up against the speaker.
The speaker's self or life as the target of hostile speech in verse 2.
An uncertain musical or performance marker preserved in the text at verses 2, 4, and 8.
A protection image used for Yahweh in verse 3.
The place from which Yahweh answers in verse 4; the chapter does not define it further.
Rescue or deliverance; verse 8 says it belongs to Yahweh.
